summary.text: The early graph depicts a wheat plant, with an upright ear, drooping leaves, stem, and roots. Shang oracle-bone inscriptions use it both for wheat and for movement; the evidence does not settle which use came first.

formation.text: A whole-graph pictograph of a wheat plant, with no separate phonetic component. One account holds that the graph was borrowed for the movement word; a competing account reverses the direction of borrowing.

components.text: The whole graph pictures a plant: the central upright shape is interpreted as its ear, the side branches as drooping leaves, and the lower strokes as stem and roots. These are parts of the picture, not separate components.

history.text: Early forms are interpreted as a branching wheat plant. Records list oracle-bone, bronze, bamboo-slip, small-seal, and Shuowen forms, but do not establish a detailed sequence of graphic changes. The seal-style form represents 來 in the Shuowen tradition.

Some analyses take an added upper stroke to distinguish wheat from movement uses. The cited early examples do not show a consistent distinction; other interpretations treat the stroke as redundant, decorative, or part of the ear.

uncertainties.text: Both wheat and movement uses occur in Shang oracle-bone material, but their relative chronology and the direction of borrowing remain unresolved.

The selected oracle and seal illustrations are modern redraws, not photographs of inscriptions or seal impressions. The seal-style image represents the Shuowen tradition and is not established as a dated stage in a graphic sequence.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A rare oracle-bone use of 來 is read as wheat. This attests the use but does not show that it was the graph’s earliest lexical use.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples use 來 for movement, including coming and going. Their chronology relative to the wheat use is unresolved.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone material also attests a return use. Its chronology and semantic relation to the other uses are unresolved.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone material; exact date unresolved
senses.text: Oracle-bone examples use 來 for tribute or bringing offerings. Their chronology and semantic relation to the other uses are unresolved.

senses.period: Oracle-bone and bronze usage; exact dates unresolved
senses.text: 來歲 means “next year” in oracle-bone and bronze usage. A connection to movement has been proposed, but no dated sequence establishes that development.
Modern dictionaries list “come” and “coming” among the character’s meanings.

limitations.text: The cited oracle-bone examples have no individual absolute dates here, so exact first-attestation dates and the relative chronology of the wheat and movement uses remain unresolved.
The chronology and pathways for return, tribute or bringing, next year, temporal “since,” and grammatical uses are not fully traced; dictionary sense lists alone do not establish their order.

items.period: Shang oracle-script style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: The branching form is conventionally interpreted as a wheat plant, with a central ear, side leaves, stem, and roots. Early inscriptions use 來 for both wheat and movement, but do not settle which use came first or the direction of borrowing.
items.alt: Black glyph with a tall central stroke, branches extending to both sides, and long strokes descending below on white.
items.selection_reason: Its visible plant-like branching shape illustrates the conventional pictographic interpretation; the evidence also shows both early uses without establishing their order or relationship.
items.rights: Commons labels the SVG representation public domain and separately records a Richard Sears courtesy/permission/copyright notice.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: This seal-style form represents 來 in the Shuowen tradition, whose account connects it with auspicious wheat and explains its movement use through wheat said to come from Heaven. That account is a historical interpretation, not confirmation of the graph’s origin.
items.alt: Black seal-style glyph with a branching upper section, a tall central stroke, and long lower strokes on white.
items.selection_reason: It illustrates the form transmitted in the Shuowen tradition and its historical explanation, without implying a proven graphic sequence or settled relation between wheat and movement.
items.rights: Commons labels the SVG representation public domain and separately records a Richard Sears courtesy/permission/copyright notice.

limitations.text: Both images are modern redraws, not photographs of ancient inscriptions or seal impressions. The seal-style form is not established as a dated stage in a graphic sequence.
